narration:
The most expensive habit I ever quit was answering immediately.

It didn't look like a habit. It looked like competence — the fast reply, the same-hour turnaround, the reputation for being on top of things. I billed it to others as reliability. But what I actually felt was a low hum of emergency that never once switched off. Not in nine years.

The economics of the instant answer are deceptive, because the cost gets booked to a different account than the benefit. The benefit lands publicly, and it lands now: the colleague unblocked, the client soothed, the thread closed. The cost lands privately, and it lands later — the decision made with the first framing that came to mind, the yes that a night's sleep would have turned into a no, and the creeping conviction, mine and everyone else's, that my time was a commons anyone could graze.

Worse than that, speed compounds into an identity. Answer fast for a year, and fast becomes your contract. The grace period other people get by default, you now have to negotiate. I had trained my whole address book, patiently, message by message, to expect of me something I did not want to give.

What finally broke the habit wasn't wisdom. It was an accident — two weeks somewhere with almost no signal. The queue that greeted my return held maybe two hundred items. Perhaps a dozen still needed me. The rest had solved themselves, or expired, or been quietly handled by people who, given a little room, turned out to be perfectly capable. Two hundred emergencies; twelve real. That ratio did more for my judgment than any book on attention I ever read — and I'd read plenty. Always quickly.

I answer slowly now. Not always, not to everything — and to genuine urgency I still move like a fire crew. But the default gap between question and answer, I've widened on purpose, and I defend it like a border. In that gap, questions ripen or they rot, and both outcomes are information. The instant answer treats every question as equally alive. The gap lets the dead ones prove that they aren't.

People ask whether the slowness costs me. Of course it costs me. It costs exactly what it looks like it costs: some shine off the reputation, some speed off the wheel. But what I bought with it is the difference between being a switchboard and being a person — and the discovery, humbling right on schedule, of how much of my necessity had only ever been decor.
